lessonTitle: Sepsis Pathophysiology: From Infection to Organ Dysfunction

blocks.text: A 52-year-old man with a perforated diverticulum has warm, flushed hands, a pulse of 120 and a blood pressure of 80/40 mmHg, even though his heart is pumping more blood per minute than normal. His circulation is not failing for lack of pump; it is failing because the vessels have lost their tone and are leaking. How does an infection in the abdomen reprogramme the whole circulation?

blocks.title: Sepsis and septic shock (Sepsis-3 definitions)
blocks.text: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection; in practice, organ dysfunction is identified as an acute increase in the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score of 2 points or more. Septic shock is a subset of sepsis in which circulatory and cellular or metabolic abnormalities are profound: persisting hypotension needing vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg, and a serum lactate above 2 mmol/L, despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

blocks.markdown: Older terminology defined sepsis as infection plus the **systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS)**, a set of non-specific features (temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, white cell count). SIRS is too sensitive and non-specific; the current emphasis is on **organ dysfunction**. The key idea is that damage comes largely from the **host's own response**, not only from the organism.

**How infection triggers the response.** The innate immune system recognises conserved microbial molecules called **pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs)** through **pattern recognition receptors (PRRs)** on macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells and endothelium. Examples: **lipopolysaccharide** (Gram-negative outer membrane) binds **Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4)**; lipoproteins and peptidoglycan-related components of Gram-positive bacteria signal through **TLR2**; **flagellin** through TLR5; bacterial **CpG DNA** through TLR9. Injured host cells also release **damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs)**, which amplify the response. Receptor activation triggers intracellular signalling (including **NF-kappa B**) and transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines: **tumour necrosis factor-alpha, interleukin-1 and interleukin-6**. These cytokines cause fever, recruit and activate neutrophils, activate coagulation and complement, and affect the vasculature.

TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6 via NF-kappa B
Nitric oxide, prostacyclin; endothelial junction disruption

blocks.title: Tracing one PAMP through the cascade
blocks.prompt: Describe how a Gram-negative bacteraemia produces fever and low blood pressure, starting from the bacterial molecule.

steps.text: LPS from the outer membrane binds TLR4 (with MD-2 and CD14) on macrophages and endothelium.
NF-kappa B signalling drives release of TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6. IL-1 and IL-6 act on the hypothalamus to cause fever.
TNF-alpha and other mediators induce inducible nitric oxide synthase and vasodilators, relaxing vascular smooth muscle, and disrupt endothelial junctions so plasma leaks.
The combination of vasodilatation and loss of plasma volume lowers blood pressure.

blocks.answer: LPS to TLR4 to cytokines to fever, vasodilatation and capillary leak, giving hypotension.

blocks.markdown: **Vasodilatation.** Cytokines and bacterial products induce **inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS)** in vascular smooth muscle and endothelium. The nitric oxide raises cyclic GMP and relaxes smooth muscle. Prostacyclin and other mediators add to this, vascular smooth muscle becomes less responsive to catecholamines and angiotensin II, and relative **vasopressin deficiency** develops. Arterial dilatation lowers **systemic vascular resistance**, and venous dilatation lowers venous return. Early in sepsis the heart compensates with tachycardia and a high cardiac output (warm shock), but cardiac output can later fall because of myocardial depression and hypovolaemia.

**Capillary leak.** Inflammation damages the **endothelial glycocalyx** (the carbohydrate-rich lining of vessels) and loosens junctions between endothelial cells. Protein-rich fluid leaves the circulation for the interstitial space, causing **oedema** and loss of effective circulating volume (relative or absolute hypovolaemia). Together with vasodilatation this explains why fluid resuscitation is needed yet may not fully restore pressure, and why oedema can impair organ function (for example in the lungs). Coagulation activation causes **microvascular thrombi**, further impairing perfusion; reduced oxygen delivery and cellular utilisation lead to **anaerobic metabolism and raised lactate**.

blocks.caption: SVR in dyn s cm^-5; MAP and CVP (central venous pressure) in mmHg; CO (cardiac output) in L/min. Reference values are commonly quoted as roughly 800-1200 and vary by source

blocks.title: Calculating systemic vascular resistance
blocks.prompt: A septic patient has MAP 60 mmHg, CVP 8 mmHg and cardiac output 9 L/min. Calculate SVR and interpret.

steps.text: This is well below the usual reference range, consistent with marked vasodilatation despite a high cardiac output.

blocks.answer: About 462 dyn s cm^-5: low resistance, reflecting vasodilatation (distributive shock).

items: Sepsis: life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to infection.
Septic shock: vasopressors needed for MAP of at least 65 mmHg and lactate above 2 mmol/L despite fluids.
PAMPs bind PRRs such as TLR4 and TLR2 and trigger TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6.
Vasodilatation: iNOS and nitric oxide, reduced vasopressor responsiveness.
Capillary leak: glycocalyx damage and loose endothelial junctions.

blocks.title: Distributive shock
blocks.text: Sepsis lowers blood pressure mainly by reducing vascular resistance and effective circulating volume, not primarily by pump failure, which is why both fluids and vasopressors may be required.

blocks.title: Definitions change
blocks.text: SIRS criteria were replaced in the Sepsis-3 consensus because they were too non-specific. Never equate fever alone with sepsis, and remember that sepsis can occur without fever, especially in the elderly.

points: Sepsis is organ dysfunction due to a dysregulated host response; septic shock needs vasopressors for MAP of at least 65 mmHg with lactate above 2 mmol/L despite fluids.
PAMPs activate pattern recognition receptors, releasing TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6.
Vasodilatation (nitric oxide) and capillary leak (glycocalyx and junction damage) cause hypotension and organ hypoperfusion.

questions.stem: According to the current (Sepsis-3) consensus, sepsis is best defined as:

options.text: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection
Any infection with a temperature above 38 degrees Celsius
A positive blood culture in any patient
A high white cell count with a normal blood pressure

questions.correctOptionText: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection

distractorRationale.b: Fever alone does not define sepsis.
distractorRationale.c: Cultures can be negative in sepsis and positive in contamination.
distractorRationale.d: A white count alone is not a definition.

questions.explanation: The definition emphasises organ dysfunction and the host response, not just infection or inflammatory signs. SOFA score change of 2 or more is used to identify organ dysfunction.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes septic shock from sepsis?

options.text: Persisting hypotension needing vasopressors to keep MAP at least 65 mmHg with lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation

questions.correctOptionText: Persisting hypotension needing vasopressors to keep MAP at least 65 mmHg with lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation

distractorRationale.b: Culture positivity is not part of the definition.
distractorRationale.c: Fever is not part of the definition.
distractorRationale.d: CRP is a marker but not part of the definition.

questions.explanation: Septic shock is sepsis with profound circulatory and metabolic abnormality. It carries a higher mortality than sepsis alone.

questions.stem: Through which receptor does lipopolysaccharide from Gram-negative bacteria trigger the innate immune response?

distractorRationale.c: The T-cell receptor recognises peptide on MHC, not LPS.
distractorRationale.d: Not an immune pattern recognition receptor.

questions.explanation: LPS, with MD-2 and CD14, activates TLR4 on macrophages and endothelial cells. This starts NF-kappa B signalling and cytokine production.

questions.stem: Which mediator is mainly responsible for vasodilatation of vascular smooth muscle in septic shock?

options.text: Nitric oxide produced by inducible nitric oxide synthase

questions.correctOptionText: Nitric oxide produced by inducible nitric oxide synthase

distractorRationale.d: Vasopressin is vasoconstrictive and relatively deficient in septic shock.

questions.explanation: Cytokines induce iNOS, producing nitric oxide that relaxes vascular smooth muscle via cyclic GMP. Vasoconstrictor responsiveness is simultaneously reduced.

questions.stem: What contributes most directly to loss of intravascular volume in sepsis?

options.text: Endothelial glycocalyx damage and disrupted junctions causing plasma leak into the interstitium

questions.correctOptionText: Endothelial glycocalyx damage and disrupted junctions causing plasma leak into the interstitium

distractorRationale.b: Not relevant to acute volume loss.

questions.explanation: Inflammation increases capillary permeability so protein-rich fluid escapes into tissues. This causes oedema and effective hypovolaemia.

questions.stem: A patient in septic shock has MAP 54 mmHg, central venous pressure 4 mmHg and cardiac output 10 L/min. Using SVR = 80 x (MAP - CVP) / CO, calculate the systemic vascular resistance in dyn s cm^-5.
questions.explanation: MAP minus CVP = 54 - 4 = 50 mmHg. SVR = 80 x 50 / 10 = 400 dyn s cm^-5, well below the usual reference range, reflecting vasodilatation with a high cardiac output.

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock has a blood pressure of 76/38 mmHg. Using MAP = (SBP + 2 x DBP) / 3, calculate the mean arterial pressure in mmHg, then state by how many mmHg it falls short of the target of 65 mmHg. Give the shortfall in mmHg.
questions.explanation: MAP = (76 + 2 x 38) / 3 = 152 / 3 = 50.7 mmHg. The shortfall from 65 mmHg is 65 - 50.7 = 14.3 mmHg, indicating inadequate perfusion pressure.

questions.stem: Define sepsis and septic shock according to current consensus, and explain why the SIRS-based definition was replaced.
markingGuide: Sepsis: life-threatening organ dysfunction due to dysregulated host response to infection (SOFA increase of 2 or more)
Septic shock: persisting hypotension requiring vasopressors for MAP at least 65 mmHg and lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids
SIRS: non-specific features (temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, white cell count) seen in many non-infectious conditions
SIRS is too sensitive and not specific; emphasis shifted to organ dysfunction
questions.explanation: The modern definition focuses on organ dysfunction rather than inflammatory signs. Septic shock represents the most severe end with circulatory and metabolic failure.

questions.stem: Explain how pathogen-associated molecular patterns trigger the systemic inflammatory response in sepsis, using a Gram-negative organism as the example.
markingGuide: PAMPs are conserved microbial molecules recognised by pattern recognition receptors
LPS (lipid A) binds TLR4 with MD-2 and CD14 on macrophages and endothelium
Signalling through NF-kappa B increases TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6
Cytokines cause fever, neutrophil activation, complement and coagulation activation, and vascular changes
DAMPs from injured host cells amplify the response; the host response contributes to organ dysfunction
questions.explanation: The innate immune system detects conserved molecules, and the resulting cytokine surge, while useful locally, becomes harmful when systemic. Both pathogen and damaged host cells contribute signals.

questions.stem: Describe how vasodilatation and capillary leak combine to cause hypotension in sepsis, and explain why the patient may have warm peripheries and a high cardiac output early on.
markingGuide: iNOS induction produces nitric oxide that relaxes vascular smooth muscle; reduced responsiveness to vasoconstrictors; relative vasopressin deficiency
Low systemic vascular resistance (arterial dilatation) and venodilatation lower venous return
Endothelial glycocalyx damage and loose junctions cause plasma leak, oedema and effective hypovolaemia
Early compensation with tachycardia and high cardiac output with vasodilated warm skin (warm shock)
Later myocardial depression and hypovolaemia may lower output; microvascular thrombosis and hypoperfusion raise lactate
questions.explanation: Both reduced vascular tone and reduced intravascular volume lower pressure. The heart compensates initially, which explains the warm high-output picture.
